children.text: Conventional scheduling orders work by deadline and by resource availability. Chapter 15 argues that a five-pillar portfolio has a third, overriding constraint: the dependency structure from Chapter 1. Each component inherits the inbound dependencies of its pillar, so an Economics component cannot be productively implemented before the Technology work that makes it measurable, however near its deadline.

This lesson explains why that constraint changes the portfolio manager's job, sets out the two decision rules the book derives from it, shows how gate status differs from a conventional critical path, and walks through what the platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test finds when it is run on Vermont's nineteen components.

The Transformation Leadership course includes a hands-on workshop that runs the same test step by step. This lesson concentrates on the scheduling logic behind it, which is what you need to apply the test to a portfolio the tool has never seen.
Why Deadlines Are the Wrong Organizing Principle

A statutory deadline tells you when something must be finished. It says nothing about whether the work it depends on will be ready in time. A portfolio scheduled by deadline alone will push hardest on whichever component is due soonest, even when that component cannot yet produce anything usable because its upstream pillar is still being built.

Chapter 15 ties this directly to the failure that opens the book. OneCare Vermont, the all-payer accountable care organization, advanced its payment model on a voluntary mandate without the integrated real-time data that would have made it manageable. In portfolio terms, an Economics component was implemented ahead of its Technology gate. The book's point is that a portfolio manager who schedules Vermont's current components by statutory date alone will reproduce exactly that failure.

The alternative is to schedule by dependency first and deadline second. The deadline still matters: it tells you how much time the dependency chain has. But the order of work comes from the chain, not from the calendar.

Design work is the important exception. Economics-as-design, the modeling and methodology that prepare a payment change, runs in parallel with Technology work. Only implementation waits for the gate (Chapter 1, §1.11.2).
Two Decision Rules a Gantt Chart Does Not Give You

The first rule: a component whose upstream pillar gate is still closed is not behind schedule. It is correctly waiting. Accelerating it consumes budget and political capital to produce output nobody can use. The book's clearest case is the AHS and Green Mountain Care Board analytics-vendor deployment, which carries the register's highest delivery-risk score, 20, tied only with the risk that the portfolio function itself is not established. It scores so high not because its own deadline is nearest, but because three downstream components converge on it.

The second rule is the inverse: a component with no unmet upstream dependency should be running now, however distant its deadline. Social-risk adjustment, the methodology that keeps global budgets from penalizing hospitals serving sicker and poorer populations, has a FY2028 target and no upstream blocker. Treating it as a FY2028 problem because that is when it is due is, in the book's words, the scheduling error that leaves equity work perpetually late.

Together the two rules reverse a common instinct. They tell the portfolio manager to relieve pressure on some components that look late and to add pressure to some that look early. Neither move makes sense on a deadline-ordered chart; both make sense once the dependencies are drawn.

children.text: Gates Versus the Critical Path

Conventional schedule analysis finds the critical path: the longest chain of linked activities, which sets the earliest possible finish. The five-pillar framework adds gates. A gate opens when the enabling work in an upstream pillar is actually finished, not when a milestone is declared (Chapter 1, §1.4). A component can sit on a schedule's critical path and still be the wrong thing to accelerate, if its gate is closed.

The book compresses this into the Portfolio Manager's Sequencing Test, four questions applied to every component in order. Which pillar does it belong to? Is that pillar's upstream gate open? If closed, what is the gating component, and is it resourced? If open, is this component running? Applied across all nineteen components, the test produces the portfolio's true critical path, which will not match the order of statutory deadlines.

The third question carries the managerial insight. When a component is waiting on a closed gate, schedule pressure belongs on the gating component, not on the waiting one. Moving pressure upstream to where the constraint actually sits is the most useful thing a portfolio manager does with a schedule.

children.text: What the Test Finds in Vermont's Portfolio

The platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test at /portfolio-sequencing-test runs these four questions on Vermont's nineteen components, using the same dependency engine as the HTR Simulator and Vermont's Fall 2026 readiness scores. With those inputs the Policy and Technology gates are open, while Economics is blocked by a Technology pillar that is only partly built, and Clinical and Operations are blocked further down the chain.

The verdicts follow. Twelve components are on track. Reference-based-pricing implementation and global-budget design are doing design work in parallel under a closed gate, which the test marks as correct. The Care Integration Network build-out is ready to implement: its gate is open but it is still in design. RHT Program deployment is implementing ahead of its gate. And three components are late by dependency order because nothing upstream is holding them and they have not started: the statewide AI-governance framework, the AHS restructuring work and the portfolio office itself.

The test also names where schedule pressure belongs. The four unfinished Technology components, the analytics deployment, the Care Integration Network, the health information exchange expansion and the AI-governance framework, each hold three Economics components waiting behind them. Those four, not the Economics components with nearer deadlines, are where a portfolio manager's attention should go.

children.text: Applying the Logic to a Portfolio of Your Own

To run the test on your own portfolio, load your inventory from Lesson 3 into the Portfolio Sequencing Test, replacing Vermont's components. For each component set its pillar and status, and decide whether its implementation genuinely needs the pillar's upstream gate. Care-model programs that produce value on their own, and analytical methodologies with no upstream blocker, are usually not gated; the tool lets you mark them so.

Then score the five pillars' current readiness, or start from the Vermont preset and adjust it. Read the verdicts in two passes. First, look for components running ahead of their gate and decide whether each is a deliberate trade-off or a mistake. Second, look at the list of components where schedule pressure belongs and compare it with where your leadership's attention actually is. The gap between those two lists is the most useful finding the test produces.

Repeat the test whenever a gate status changes. A portfolio's critical path moves as upstream work finishes, and the components that were correctly waiting last quarter may be late this quarter if they did not start when their gate opened.
